questions.question: The temperature of a body in air falls from $40^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $24^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ in 4 minutes. The temperature of the air is $16^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. The temperature of the body in the next 4 minutes will be:
questions.explanation: $\begin{aligned} & \Delta T=T_2-T_1=16^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \\ & \text { And } T_0=16^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \\ & \frac{\Delta T}{t_1}=-k\left(32-16^{\circ}\right)...(i) \\ & \frac{\left(24-T_3\right)}{4}=-k\left(\frac{24+T_3}{2}-16\right) ....(ii) \\ & \frac{16}{4}=-k(16) \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{\left(24-T_3\right)}{4}=-k\left(12+\frac{T_3}{2}-16\right) \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{16}{24-T_3}=\frac{16}{T_3} T_2 \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{T_3}{2}-4=24-T_3 \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{3 T_3}{2}=28 \\ & \Rightarrow T_3=\frac{56}{3}{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \end{aligned}$ ,

questions.question: The graph between two temperature scales $P$ and $Q$ is shown in the figure. Between upper fixed point and lower fixed point there are $150$ equal divisions of scale $P$ and $100$ divisions on scale $Q$. The relationship for conversion between the two scales is given by : .
questions.explanation:
From the graph

For scale $P$,

Lower fixed point$= 180 - 150 = 30 ^\circ P$

Upper fixed point$= 180 ^\circ P$

For scale $Q$,

Lower fixed point$= 0 ^\circ Q$

Upper fixed point$= 100 ^\circ Q$

Thus, the relationship between the two scales $P$ and $Q$ is given by

$\frac{{t}_{P} - 30}{180 - 30} = \frac{{t}_{Q} - 0}{100 - 0} \implies \frac{{t}_{P}}{ - } = \frac{{t}_{Q}}{100}$

,

questions.question: On a temperature scale '$X$', the boiling point of water is $65 ^\circ X$ and the freezing point is $- 15 ^\circ X$. Assuming that the $X$ scale is linear. The equivalent temperature corresponding to $- 95 ^\circ X$ on the Fahrenheit scale would be
questions.explanation:
The relation between two temperature scales can be written as follows

$\frac{65 - x}{65 - \left( - 15\right)} = \frac{212 - F}{180}...\left(1\right)$

Substitute the values of the known parameters in to equation (1) and sole to calculate the required temperature in Fahrenheit scale.

$\begin{matrix}\frac{65 + 95}{80} & = & \frac{212 - F}{180} \\ & \implies & 2 \times 180 = 212 - F \\ & \implies & F = 212 - 360 \\ & = & - 148 ^\circ F\end{matrix}$

;

questions.question: A faulty thermometer reads $5 ^\circ C$ in melting ice and $95 ^\circ C$ in steam. The correct temperature on absolute scale will be ______ $K$ when the faulty thermometer reads $41 ^\circ C$.
questions.explanation:
As per working of thermometers, $\frac{X - LFP}{UFP - LFP} = \text{constant}$.

Therefore, we can write

$\frac{41 ^\circ - 5 ^\circ }{95 ^\circ - 5 ^\circ } = \frac{C - 0 ^\circ }{100 ^\circ - 0 ^\circ } \implies C = \frac{36}{90} \times 100\;$

questions.question: A thermometer graduated according to a linear scale reads a value $x_{0}$ when in contact with boiling water, and $x_{0} / 3$ when in contact with ice. What is the temperature of an object in ${ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, if this thermometer in the contact with the object reads $x_{0} / 2 ?$
questions.explanation: Let required temperature $=\mathrm{T}^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ $\Rightarrow \mathrm{T}^{\circ} \mathrm{C}=\frac{\mathrm{x}_{0}}{2}-\frac{\mathrm{x}_{0}}{3}=\frac{\mathrm{x}_{0}}{6} \&\left(\mathrm{x}_{0}-\frac{\mathrm{x}_{0}}{3}\right)=\left(100-0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right) \Rightarrow \frac{2 \mathrm{x}_{0}}{3}=100 \Rightarrow \mathrm{x}_{0}=\frac{300}{2} \Rightarrow \mathrm{T}^{\circ} \mathrm{C}=\frac{\mathrm{x}_{0}}{6}=\frac{150}{6}=25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$

questions.question: An ideal gas is expanding such that $P{T}^{3} =$ constant. The coefficient of volume expansion of the gas is:
questions.explanation:
$\gamma = \frac{1}{V}\frac{dV}{dt} P{T}^{3} =$ constant

$\frac{T}{V}{T}^{3} =$ Constant

${T}^{4}{V}^{ - 1} = C {V}^{ - 1}\left(4{T}^{3}dT\right) + {T}^{4}\left(\frac{ - 1}{{V}^{2}}dV\right) = 0 \frac{dV}{dT} = \frac{4{T}^{3} / V}{{T}^{4} / {V}^{2}} = \frac{4V}{T}∴\gamma = \frac{4}{T}$

questions.question: Two different wires having lengths ${L}_{1}$ and ${L}_{2}$ and respective temperature coefficient of linear expansion ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{2},$ are joined end-to-end. Then the effective temperature coefficient of linear expansion is :
questions.explanation:
The wire are joined end-to-end, so they are in series combination, then total length of wire is given by

$L = {L}_{1} + {L}_{2}...(1)$

When the temperature is increase by $\Delta \theta$, then its final length is given by using concept of linear expansion,

${L}^{'} = L(1 + \alpha \Delta \theta )...(2)$

Using equation $(1)$ and $(2)$ for the series combination of wires, final length is given by

${L}^{'} = {{L}_{1}}^{'} + {{L}_{2}}^{'}...(3) \implies \left({L}_{1} + {L}_{2}\right)(1 + {\alpha }_{\mathrm{eff}} \Delta \theta ) = {L}_{1}(1 + {\alpha }_{1} \Delta \theta ) + {L}_{2}(1 + {\alpha }_{2} \Delta \theta ) \implies {\alpha }_{\mathrm{eff}} = \frac{{L}_{1}{\alpha }_{1} + {L}_{2}{\alpha }_{2}}{\left({L}_{1} + {L}_{2}\right)}$

questions.question: A bimetallic strip consists of metals $A$ and $B$. It is mounted rigidly as shown. The metal $A$ has higher coefficient of expansion compared to that of metal $B$. When the bimetallic strip is placed in a cold both, it will :
questions.explanation: ${\alpha }_{A} > {\alpha }_{B}$ Length of both strips will decrease $\Delta {L}_{A} > \Delta {L}_{B}$

questions.question:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion $A$ and the other is labelled as Reason $R$.

Assertion $A$ : When a rod lying freely is heated, no thermal stress is developed in it.

Reason $R$ : On heating, the length of the rod increases.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Both $A$ and $R$ are true and $R$ is the correct explanation of $A$
Both $A$ and $R$ are true but $R$ is NOT the correct explanation of $A$
questions.explanation:
Thermal stress is mechanical stress created by any change in temperature of a material. When the body is under some constraints, thermal stress is generated. But if it is lying freely, no thermal stress is developed.

The increase in length of a body with temperature is given by

$\Delta L = L\alpha \Delta T$

So, with the increase in temperature, the length of the rod increases.

$A$ and $R$ are true but $R$ is not the correct explanation of $A$.

:

questions.question: Two thin metallic spherical shells of radii ${r}_{1}$ and ${r}_{2}\left({r}_{1} < {r}_{2}\right)$ are placed with their centres coinciding. A material of thermal conductivity $K$ is filled in the space between the shells. The inner shell is maintained at temperature ${\theta }_{1}$ and the outer shell at temperature ${\theta }_{2}\left({\theta }_{1} < {\theta }_{2}\right).$ The rate at which heat flows radially through the material is :
questions.explanation: Equivalent resistance $(R) = \frac{{r}_{2} - {r}_{1}}{K4\pi {r}_{2}{r}_{1}}$ Thus, Heat flow $= \frac{4\pi K\left({r}_{1}{r}_{2}\right)\left({\theta }_{2} - {\theta }_{1}\right)}{\left({r}_{2} - {r}_{1}\right)}$ !

questions.question: A bakelite beaker has volume capacity of $500\mathrm{cc}$ at $30 ^\circ C$. When it is partially filled with ${V}_{m}$ volume (at $30 ^\circ C$) of mercury, it is found that the unfilled volume of the beaker remains constant as temperature is varied. If ${\gamma }_{\text{bester }} = 6 \times {10}^{ - 6}0 ^\circ {C}^{ - 1},$ where $\gamma$ is the coefficient of volume expansion, then ${V}_{m}$ (in $\mathrm{cc}$ ) is close to $\dots$
questions.explanation: $\Delta \mathrm{Vm} = \Delta \mathrm{Vc} \mathrm{Vmγm} \Delta T = \mathrm{Vcγc} \Delta T \mathrm{Vm} = \frac{\mathrm{Vcγc}}{\mathrm{γm}} = \frac{500 \times 6 \times {10}^{ - 6}}{1.5. \times {10}^{ - 4}} = 20\mathrm{cc}$

questions.question: A uniform cylindrical rod of length $L$ and radius r, is made from a material whose Young’s modulus of Elasticity equals $Y.$ When this rod is heated by temperature T and simultaneously subjected to a net longutudinal compressional force F, its length remains unchanged. The coefficient of volume expansion, of the material of the rod, is (nearly) equal to:
questions.explanation: Stress $= \frac{F}{A} Y\left(\alpha T\right) = \frac{F}{A} \alpha = \frac{F}{A\left(YT\right)} \gamma = 3\alpha = \frac{3F}{AYT} \gamma = \frac{3F}{\pi {r}^{2}YT}$

questions.question: When the temperature of a metal wire is increased from $0ºC\mathrm{to}10ºC$, its length increases by $0.02%$.The percentage change in its mass density will be closed to:
questions.explanation:
$\Delta ℓ = ℓ\alpha \Delta t \alpha = \frac{\Delta ℓ}{ℓ\Delta T} = \frac{0.02}{100 \times 10};\alpha = 2 \times {10}^{ - 5} \gamma = 3\alpha = 6 \times {10}^{ - 5} \frac{\Delta V}{V} = \gamma \times \Delta T;\frac{\Delta V}{V} \times 100 = \left(6 \times {10}^{ - 5} \times 10 \times 100\right) = 6 \times {10}^{ - 2}$

Volume increase by $0.06%$ therefore density decrease by $0.06%$

questions.question: Each side of a box made of metal sheet in cubic shape is $a$ at room temperature $T$, the coefficient of linear expansion of the metal sheet is $\alpha$. The metal sheet is heated uniformly, by a small temperature $\Delta T$, so that its new temperature is $T + \Delta T$. Calculate the increase in the volume of the metal box.
questions.explanation: $\Delta V = V\gamma \Delta T \Delta V = 3{a}^{3}\alpha \Delta T$

questions.question: Two rods $A$ and $B$ of identical dimensions are at temperature $30^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. If $\mathrm{A}$ is heated upto $180^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and $\mathrm{B}$ upto $\mathrm{T}^{\circ} \mathrm{C},$ then the new lengths are the same. If the ratio of the coefficients of linear expansion of $\mathrm{A}$ and $\mathrm{B}$ is $4: 3,$ then the value of $T$ is
questions.explanation:
Change in length in both rods are same i.e.

$\Delta \ell_{1}=\Delta \ell_{2} \ell \alpha_{1} \Delta \theta_{1}=\ell \alpha_{2} \Delta \theta_{2}$

$\begin{array}{l}

$\frac${$\$alpha_{1} }{$\$alpha_{2} }=$\frac${$\Delta \$theta_{2} }{$\Delta$ \$theta_{1} } $\quad$\left[$\because \frac${$\$alpha_{1} }{$\$alpha_{2} }=$\frac{4}{3}$\right]$ \\

$\frac{4}{3} = \frac{\theta-30}{180-30}$

\end{array}$

$\theta=230^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ ,

questions.question: A solid metallic cube having total surface area $24{m}^{2}$ is uniformly heated. If its temperature is increased by $10 ^\circ C$, calculate the increase in volume of the cube. (Given $\alpha = 5.0 \times {10}^{ - 4}{C}^{∘ - 1}$).
questions.explanation:
Total surface area of a cube is $6{a}^{2} = 24{m}^{2} \implies {a}^{2} = 4 \implies a = 2m$

Volume of a cube $V = {a}^{3} = 8{m}^{3}$

Change in volume is given by,

$\Delta V = {V}_{0}\gamma \Delta T$, where $\gamma = 3\alpha \Delta V = \left(8\right) \times \left(1.5 \times {10}^{ - 4}\right) \times \left(10\right){m}^{3} \implies \Delta V = 1.2 \times {10}^{5}{\mathrm{cm}}^{3}$

`

questions.question:
At what temperature a gold ring of diameter $6.230\mathrm{cm}$ be heated so that it can be fitted on a wooden bangle of diameter $6.241\mathrm{cm}$? Both the diameters have been measured at room temperature $\left(27 ^\circ C\right)$.

(Given: coefficient of linear thermal expansion of gold ${\alpha }_{L} = 1.4 \times {10}^{ - 5}{K}^{ - 1}$)
questions.explanation:
To fit gold ring of diameter $5.230\mathrm{cm}$ over wooden bangle of diameter $6.241\mathrm{cm}$, gold ring expansion is required.

So, $l = {l}_{0}\left(1 + \alpha \Delta T\right) \implies 6.241 = 6.230\left(1 + 1.4 \times {10}^{ - 5}\left(T - 27\right)\right) \implies \frac{6.241}{6.230} - 1 = 1.4 \times {10}^{ - 5}\left(T - 27\right) \implies T = 152.7 ^\circ C$

!

questions.question: A hole is drilled in a metal sheet. At $27 ^\circ C$, the diameter of hole is $5\mathrm{cm}$. When the sheet is heated to $177 ^\circ C$, the change in the diameter of hole is $d \times {10}^{ - 3}\mathrm{cm}$ . The value of $d$ will be _____, if coefficient of linear expansion of the metal is $1.6 \times {10}^{ - 5} / C∘$
questions.explanation:
Expansion of hole will be similar to that of an imaginary disc.

Let diameter be ${d}_{0}$ at $27 ^\circ C$ and ${d}^{'}$ at $177 ^\circ C$. Therefore, we can write

${d}^{'} = {d}_{0}\left(1 + \alpha \Delta T\right)$

Therefore, change in diameter will be

$\implies {d}^{'} - {d}_{0} = \left(5\right) \times \left(1.6 \times {10}^{ - 5}\right) \times \left(177 - 27\right) = 12 \times {10}^{ - 3}\mathrm{cm}$

Hence, required value of $d = 12$.

questions.question:
A unit scale is to be prepared whose length does not change with temperature and remains $20\mathrm{cm}$, using a bimetallic strip made of brass and iron each of different length. The length of both components would change in such a way that difference between their lengths remains constant. If length of brass is $40\mathrm{cm}$ and length of iron will be _____ $\mathrm{cm}$.

$\left({\alpha }_{\mathrm{iron}} = 1.2 \times {10}^{ - 5}{K}^{ - 1}\right)$ and $\left({\alpha }_{\mathrm{brass}} = 1.8 \times {10}^{ - 5}{K}^{ - 1}\right)$.
questions.explanation:
Linear expansion of solid with temperature is given by ${L}_{f} = {L}_{0}\left(1 + \alpha \Delta T\right)$

Here, ${l}_{B}\left(1 + {\alpha }_{B}\Delta T\right) - {l}_{i}\left(1 + {\alpha }_{i}\Delta T\right) = {l}_{B} - {l}_{i} \implies {\alpha }_{B}{l}_{B} = {l}_{i}{\alpha }_{i} \implies 1.8 \times {10}^{ - 5} \times 40 = {l}_{i} \times 1.2 \times {10}^{ - 5} \implies {l}_{i} = \frac{1.8 \times {10}^{ - 5} \times 40}{1.2 \times {10}^{ - 5}} = \frac{3 \times 40}{2} = 60 \implies {l}_{i} = 60\mathrm{cm}$

questions.question:
$1\mathrm{kg}$ of water, at $20 ^\circ C$ is heated in an electric kettle whose heating element has a mean (temperature averaged) resistance of $20\text{ }\Omega .$ The rms voltage in the mains is $200V$. Ignoring heat loss from the kettle, time taken for water to evaporate fully is close to

[ Specific heat of water $= 4200J{\mathrm{kg}}^{ - 1} ^\circ {C}^{ - 1}$ Latent heat of water $= 2260kJk{g}^{ - 1}$ ]
questions.explanation:
Given specific heat of the water $4200J{\mathrm{kg}}^{ - 1} ^\circ {C}^{ - 1}$

Latent heat of the water $= 2260\text{ }kJk{g}^{ - 1} Q = P \times t Q = mc\Delta T + mL \implies P \times t = mc\Delta T + mL \implies \frac{{V}_{rms}^{2}}{R} \times t = mc\Delta T + mL \implies \frac{{\left(200\right)}^{2}}{20} \times t = 4200 \times 80 + 2260 \times {10}^{3} \implies t = 1298\text{ s}≃22\text{ }min$

questions.question:
Heat energy of $184\mathrm{kJ}$ is given to ice of mass $600g$ at $- 12 ^\circ C$, Specific heat of ice is $2222.3J{\mathrm{kg}}^{–1} ^\circ {C}^{–1}$ and latent heat of ice is $336\mathrm{kJ}{\mathrm{kg}}^{–1}$.

(A) Final temperature of system will be $0 ^\circ C$

(B) Final temperature of the system will be greater than $0 ^\circ C$

(C) The final system will have a mixture of ice and water in the ratio of $5 : 1$

(D) The final system will have a mixture of ice and water in the ratio of $1 : 5$

(E) The final system will have water only

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Given:

$\Delta Q = 184 \times {10}^{3}J$,

$m = 0.600\mathrm{kg}\text{at} - 12 ^\circ C$,

$S = 2222.3J{\mathrm{kg}}^{–1} ^\circ {C}^{–1}$ and

$L = 336 \times {10}^{3}J{\mathrm{kg}}^{ - 1}$

Heat required to convert ice from $–12 ^\circ C$ to ice at $0 ^\circ C$ will be,

${Q}_{1} = 0.600 \times 2222.3 \times 12 = 16000.56J$

Remaining heat $Q = 184000 - 16000.56 = 167999.44J$

Heat required to melt ice completely at $0 ^\circ C$,

${Q}_{2} = 0.600 \times 336000 = 201600J$ needed which is more than $Q$, so $100%$ ice is not melted.

For amount of melted ice, we can write

$167999.44 = m \times 336000\; ∴$ mass of water $= 0.4999kg$

Mass of ice remaining $= 0.1001 ∴$ Ratio $= \frac{0.1001}{0.4999} \approx 1 : 5$

questions.question: A calorimeter of water equivalent $20g$ contains $180g$ of water at $25 ^\circ C$. $m''$' grams of steam at $100 ^\circ C$ is mixed in it till the temperature of the mixture is $31 ^\circ C$. The value of $m''$ is close to (Latent heat of water$= 540\mathrm{cal}{g}^{ - 1}$, specific heat of water$= 1\mathrm{cal}{g}^{ - 1 ^\circ }{C}^{ - 1}$)
questions.explanation: $\left(200\right)\left(31 - 25\right) = m \times 540 + m\left(1\right)\left(69\right) 1200 = m\left(609\right) m \approx 2$

questions.question: A $100g$ of iron nail is hit by a $1.5\mathrm{kg}$ hammer striking at a velocity of $60{\mathrm{ms}}^{ - 1}$. What will be the rise in the temperature of the nail if one fourth of energy of the hammer goes into heating the nail ? [Specific heat capacity of iron $= 0.42{\mathrm{Jg}}^{ - 1}{C}^{∘ - 1}$]
questions.explanation:
If we heat-up an object, then, the energy is used to either change the temperature of the body or to change the state of the body.

If it changes the temperature, then,

$Q = mS \Delta T$

where, $Q$ is the heat given, $m$ is the mass and $\Delta T$ is the change in temperature.

We know that a moving object has an energy in the form of kinetic energy, i.e.,

$KE = \frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2}$

When that moving object strikes another object, it loses some energy which changes into the heat energy and this heat energy increases the temperature of the object.

Given a hammer of $1.5\mathrm{kg}$ is moving with $60m{s}^{ - 1}$.

Kinetic energy $= \frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2} = \frac{1}{2}(1.5)(60{)}^{2} = 2700J$

One-fourth of kinetic energy changes into heat energy.

$\implies \frac{1}{4}(KE) =$ Heat energy

$\implies \frac{1}{4}(KE) = m(S)( \Delta T) \implies \frac{1}{4}(2700) = (100)(0.42)( \Delta T) \implies \Delta T = 16.07 ^\circ C$

;

questions.question: A block of ice at $- 10 ^\circ C$ is slowly heated and converted to steam at $100 ^\circ C$. Which of the following curves represent the phenomenon qualitatively:
questions.explanation:
When the state of the substance is not changing, temperature of the substance increases when heat is supplied to it. But when the substance changes the state, the heat supplied to it used as latent heat and the temperature remains constant until all the substance converts to other state.

Therefore, temperature of ice first increases from $- 10 ^\circ C$ to $0 ^\circ C$. Then, remains constant at $0 ^\circ C$ till whole ice is melted. Then, it increases from $0 ^\circ C$ to $100 ^\circ C$. Again it remains constant at $100 ^\circ C$ till whole water converts into steam.

!

questions.question:
A geyser heats water flowing at a rate of $2.0\mathrm{kg}$ per minute from $30 ^\circ C$ to $70 ^\circ C$. If geyser operates on a gas burner, the rate of combustion of fuel will be _____ $g{\min }^{ - 1}$.

[Heat of combustion $= 8 \times {10}^{3}{\mathrm{Jg}}^{ - 1}$, Specific heat of water $= 4.2{\mathrm{Jg}}^{ - 1}{C}^{∘ - 1}$]
questions.explanation:
Given here, mass flow rate of water, $\frac{dm}{dt} = 2\mathrm{kg}{\min }^{ - 1}$

The geyser heats the water, raising the temperature from ${\theta }_{1} = 30 ^\circ C$ to ${\theta }_{2} = 70 ^\circ C$.

Total heat utilised in raising the temperature, $\frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t} = \frac{dm}{dt} \times s\Delta \theta \frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t} = \frac{2}{60} \times 4.2 \times 40 = \frac{m}{t} \times L L =$ heat of combination$= 8 \times {10}^{3}J{g}^{ - 1}$

Now, rate of consumption of fuel is $\frac{m}{t} = \frac{2 \times 4.2 \times 40}{60 \times 8 \times {10}^{3}} = \frac{4.2}{6} \times {10}^{ - 3} = 0.7 \times {10}^{ - 3}\mathrm{kg}{\sec }^{ - 1} = 42g{\min }^{ - 1}$

questions.question: A cylinder of fixed capacity of $44.8$ litres contains helium gas at standard temperature and pressure. The amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of gas in the cylinder by $20.0 ^\circ C$ will be (Given gas constant $R = 8.3J{K}^{ - 1}{\mathrm{mol}}^{ - 1}$)
questions.explanation:
At STP volume occupied by one mole of a gas is $22.4L$. Therefore, number of moles are, $n = \frac{44.8}{22.4} = 2\mathrm{mol}$.

The process is isochoric process as the volume of the cylinder remains fixed and helium is a monatomic gas. Therefore, amount of heat needed will be,

$Q = nCv\Delta T = \left(2\right)\left(\frac{3}{2}R\right)\left(20\right) = 3 \times 8.3 \times 20 = 498J$

questions.question: An amount of ice of mass $10^{-3} \mathrm{~kg}$ and temperature $-10^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ is transformed to vapour of temperature $110^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ by applying heat. The total amount of work required for this conversion is, (Take, specific heat of ice $=2100 \mathrm{Jkg}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$, specific heat of water $=4180 \mathrm{Jkg}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$, specific heat of steam $=1920 \mathrm{Jkg}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$, Latent heat of ice $=3.35 \times 10^5 \mathrm{Jkg}^{-1}$ and Latent heat of steam $=2.25 \times 10^6 \mathrm{Jkg}^{-1}$ )
questions.explanation: $\begin{aligned} & \Delta \mathrm{Q}_1=\mathrm{m} \times \mathrm{S}_1 \times \Delta \mathrm{T}=10^{-3} \times 2100 \times 10=21 \mathrm{~J} \\ & \Delta \mathrm{Q}_2=\mathrm{m} \times \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{f}}=10^{-3} \times 3.35 \times 10^5=335 \mathrm{~J} \\ & \Delta \mathrm{Q}_3=\mathrm{m} \times \mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{w}} \times \Delta \mathrm{T}=10^{-3} \times 4180 \times 100=418 \mathrm{~J} \\ & \Delta \mathrm{Q}_4=\mathrm{m} \times \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{v}}=10^{-3} \times 2.25 \times 10^6=2250 \mathrm{~J} \\ & \Delta \mathrm{Q}_5=\mathrm{m} \times \mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{v}} \times \Delta \mathrm{T}=10^{-3} \times 1920 \times 10=19.2 \mathrm{~J} \\ & \Delta \mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{net}}=3043.2 \mathrm{~J}\end{aligned}$

questions.question: $1\mathrm{kg}$ of water at $100 ^\circ C$ is converted into steam at $100 ^\circ C$ by boiling at atmospheric pressure. The volume of water changes from $1.00 \times {10}^{ - 3}{m}^{3}$ as a liquid to $1.671{m}^{3}$ as steam. The change in internal energy of the system during the process will be (Given latent heat of vaporisation $= 2257\mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg}$, Atmospheric pressure $\left( = 1 \times {10}^{5}\mathrm{Pa}\right)$
questions.explanation:
The work to be done in the process is given by

$\begin{matrix}dW & = & PdV \\ = 1 \times {10}^{5}\mathrm{Pa} \times (1.671 - 0.001){m}^{3} \\ = 1.670 \times {10}^{5}J\end{matrix}$

The change in heat energy during the vaporisation process can be calculated as follows-

$\begin{matrix}\Delta {Q}_{\text{supplied }} & = & 2257 \times 1 \times {10}^{3}J \\ = 22.57 \times {10}^{5}J\end{matrix}$

Hence, the change in internal energy in the process is given by

$\begin{matrix}\Delta U & = & \Delta {Q}_{\mathrm{supplied}} - \Delta W \\ = (22.57 - 1.67) \times {10}^{5}J \\ = 20.9 \times {10}^{5}J \\ = 2090\mathrm{kJ}\end{matrix}$

questions.question: A gun fires a lead bullet of temperature 300 K into a wooden block. The bullet having melting temperature of 600 K penetrates into the block and melts down. If the total heat required for the process is 625 J , then the mass of the bullet is $\qquad$ grams. (Latent heat of fusion of lead $=2.5 \times 10^4 \mathrm{JKg}^{-1}$ and specific heat capacity of lead $=125 \mathrm{JKg}^{-1} \left.\mathrm{K}^{-1}\right)$
questions.explanation: $\begin{aligned} & 625=\mathrm{ms} \Delta \mathrm{T}+\mathrm{mL} \\ & 625=\mathrm{m}\left[125 \times 300+2.5 \times 10^4\right] \\ & 625=\mathrm{m}[37500+25000] \\ & 625=\mathrm{m}[62500] \\ & \mathrm{m}=\frac{1}{100} \mathrm{~kg} \\ & \mathrm{M}=10 \text { grams }\end{aligned}$ .

questions.question: The temperature of equal masses of three different liquids $x,y$ and $z$ are $10 ^\circ C,20 ^\circ C$ and $30 ^\circ C$ respectively. The temperature of mixture when $x$ is mixed with $y$ is $16 ^\circ C$ and that when $y$ is mixed with $z$ is $26 ^\circ C$. The temperature of mixture when $x$ and $z$ are mixed will be :

Two identical beakers $A$ and $B$ contain equal volumes of two different liquids at $60 ^\circ C$ each and left to cool down. Liquid in $A$ has density of $8 \times {10}^{2}kg{m}^{ - 3}$ and specific heat of $2000Jk{g}^{ - 1}{K}^{ - 1}$ while the liquid in $B$ has density ${10}^{3}kg{m}^{ - 3}$ and specific heat of $4000Jk{g}^{ - 1}{K}^{ - 1}$. Which of the following best describes their temperature versus time graph schematically? (assume the emissivity of both the beakers to be the same)
questions.explanation:
From Newton's law of cooling,

Rate of cooling: $\left( - \frac{dT}{dt}\right) = \frac{4\sigma eA{T}_{0}^{3}\left(T - {T}_{0}\right)}{ms} \propto \frac{1}{ms}$** **

$∴{\rho }_{A} < {\rho }_{B} {m}_{A} < {m}_{B}$

And ${s}_{A} < {s}_{B} {m}_{A}{s}_{A} < {m}_{B}{s}_{B}$

At $t = 0,{\left( - \frac{dT}{dt}\right)}_{A} > {\left( - \frac{dT}{dt}\right)}_{B}$

Initially, the rate of cooling for $A$ will be higher than $B$ and temperature $(T)$ vs time $(t)$ graph will be a curve. !

questions.question: According to law of equipartition of energy the molar specific heat of a diatomic gas at constant volume where the molecule has one additional vibrational mode is :-
questions.explanation:
A diatomic gas has 5 degrees of freedom apart from vibrational degree of freedom. For each additional vibrational mode, degree of freedom is increased by $2$. So new degree of freedom,

$f = 5 + 2 = 7$

Therefore, we require molar specific heat capacity at constant volume, which is given by

${C}_{v} = \frac{f}{2}R = \frac{7}{2}R$

questions.question:
Three containers ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ have water at different temperatures. The table below shows the final temperature $T$ when different amounts of water (given in liters) are taken from each container and mixed (assume no loss of heat during the process)
${C}_{1}$ ${C}_{2}$ ${C}_{3}$ $T$
$1l$ $2l$ $- -$ ${60}^{o}C$
$- -$ $1l$ $2l$ ${30}^{o}C$
$2l$ $- -$ $1l$ ${60}^{o}C$
$1l$ $1l$ $1l$ $\theta$
The value of $\theta$ (in ${}^{o}C$ to the nearest integer) is___________
questions.explanation:
Let ${\theta }_{1}$, ${\theta }_{2}$ and ${\theta }_{3}$ be the temperatures of water in three containers.

$1{\theta }_{1} + 2{\theta }_{2} + 0{\theta }_{3} = \left(1 + 2\right)60 {\theta }_{1} + 2{\theta }_{2} = 180$ …. (1)

$0 \times {\theta }_{1} + 1 \times {\theta }_{2} + 2 \times {\theta }_{3} = \left(1 + 2\right)30 {\theta }_{2} + 2{\theta }_{3} = 90$ …… (2)

$2 \times {\theta }_{1} + 0 \times {\theta }_{2} + 1 \times {\theta }_{3} = \left(2 + 1\right)60 2{\theta }_{1} + {\theta }_{3} = 180$ …. (3)

and ${\theta }_{1} + {\theta }_{2} + {\theta }_{3} = \left(1 + 1 + 1\right)\theta$

from (1)+(2)+(3)

$3{\theta }_{1} + 3{\theta }_{2} + 3{\theta }_{3} = 450⟹{\theta }_{1} + {\theta }_{2} + {\theta }_{3} = 150$

from (4) equation $150 = 3\theta ⟹\theta = 50 ^\circ C$

questions.question:
A water heater of power $2000W$ is used to heat water. The specific heat capacity of water is $4200J{\mathrm{kg}}^{ - 1}{K}^{ - 1}$. The efficiency of heater is $70%$. Time required to heat $2\mathrm{kg}$ of water from $10 ^\circ C$ to $60 ^\circ C$ is _____ $s$.

(Assume that the specific heat capacity of water remains constant over the temperature range of the water).
questions.explanation:
Heat provided to water will be responsible for increase in temperature. Therefore, we can write

$\eta \times P \times t = M \times s \times \Delta T$

Now, $\eta = \frac{70}{100} = 0.7$ and $\text{energy} = \text{power} \times \text{time}$.

Therefore,

$t = \frac{2 \times 4200 \times \left(60 ^\circ - 10 ^\circ \right)}{0.7 \times 2000}s = 300s$

questions.question: Two metallic wires of identical dimensions are connected is series. If ${\sigma }_{1}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}$ are the conductivities of the these wires respectively, the effective conductivity of the combination is :
questions.explanation: Let length of wire be $l$, Area of wire as $A$ For equivalent wire length $= 2l$ & area will be $A$ As the wires are connected in series combination, the thermal resistance ${R}_{eq} = {R}_{1} + {R}_{2} \implies \frac{2l}{{\sigma }_{\mathrm{eq}}A} = \frac{l}{{\sigma }_{1}A} + \frac{l}{{\sigma }_{1}A} \implies \frac{2}{{\sigma }_{\mathrm{eq}}} = \frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}} + \frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}\;$

questions.question: Temperature difference of ${120}^{o}C$ is maintained between two ends of a uniform rod $AB$ of length $2L.$ Another bent rod $PQ,$ of same cross-section as $AB$ and length $\frac{3L}{2},$ is connected across $AB$ (See figure). In steady state, temperature difference between $P$ and $Q$ will be close to:
questions.explanation: ${T}_{1} - {T}_{2} = {120}^{o}C$ We define thermal resistance $R = \frac{L}{KA}$ Given circuit can be reduced to Equivalent resistance ${R}_{eq} = \frac{8R}{5}$ Thermal current $i = \frac{{T}_{1} - {T}_{2}}{\frac{8R}{5}} {T}_{P} - {T}_{Q} = \frac{{T}_{1} - {T}_{2}}{\left(\frac{8R}{5}\right)}\left(\frac{3R}{5}\right) = \frac{3}{8} \times 120 = 45$

questions.question: The temperature $\theta$ at the junction of two insulating sheets, having thermal resistances ${R}_{1}$ and ${R}_{2}$ as well as top and bottom temperatures ${\theta }_{1}$ and ${\theta }_{2}$ (as shown in figure) is given by :
questions.explanation: Heat flow rate will be same through both $∴\frac{{\theta }_{1} - \theta }{{R}_{1}} = \frac{\theta - {\theta }_{2}}{{R}_{2}} {R}_{2}{\theta }_{1} - {R}_{2}\theta = {R}_{1}\theta - {R}_{1}{\theta }_{2} \theta = \frac{{R}_{2}{\theta }_{1} + {R}_{1}{\theta }_{2}}{{R}_{1} + {R}_{2}}$ .

questions.question: Two conductors have the same resistances at $0 ^\circ C$ but their temperature coefficients of resistance are ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{2}$. The respective temperature coefficients for their series and parallel combinations are :
questions.explanation:
Change in resistance due to temperature is given by, ${R}^{'} = R\left(1 + \alpha \Delta T\right)$

For Series Combination:

${R}_{eq} = {R}_{1} + {R}_{2} \implies 2R\left(1 + {\alpha }_{eq} \Delta T\right) = R\left(1 + {\alpha }_{1} \Delta T\right) + R\left(1 + {\alpha }_{2} \Delta T\right) \implies 2R\left(1 + {\alpha }_{eq} \Delta T\right) = 2R + \left({\alpha }_{1} + {\alpha }_{2}\right)R \Delta T \implies {\alpha }_{eq} = \frac{{\alpha }_{1} + {\alpha }_{2}}{2}$

For Parallel Combination:

$\frac{1}{{R}_{eq}} = \frac{1}{{R}_{1}} + \frac{1}{{R}_{2}} \implies \frac{1}{\frac{R}{2}} = \frac{1}{R} + \frac{1}{R} \implies \frac{2}{1 + {\alpha }_{eq} \Delta T} = \frac{1}{1} + \frac{1}{1} \implies \frac{2}{1 + {\alpha }_{eq} \Delta T} = \frac{1 + {\alpha }_{2} \Delta T + 1 + {\alpha }_{1} \Delta T}{\left(1 + {\alpha }_{1} \Delta T\right)\left(1 + {\alpha }_{2} \Delta T\right)} \implies 2\left(\left(1 + {\alpha }_{1} \Delta T\right)\left(1 + {\alpha }_{2} \Delta T\right)\right) = \left(2 + \left({\alpha }_{1} + {\alpha }_{2}\right) \Delta T\right)\left(1 + {\alpha }_{eq} \Delta T\right) \implies 2\left(1 + {\alpha }_{1} \Delta T + {\alpha }_{2} \Delta T + {\alpha }_{1}{\alpha }_{2} \Delta T\right) = 2 + 2{\alpha }_{eq} \Delta T + \left({\alpha }_{1} + {\alpha }_{2}\right) \Delta T + {\alpha }_{eq}\left({\alpha }_{1} + {\alpha }_{2}\right) \Delta {T}^{2}$

Neglecting small terms

$2 + 2\left({\alpha }_{1} + {\alpha }_{2}\right) \Delta T = 2 + 2{\alpha }_{eq} \Delta T + \left({\alpha }_{1} + {\alpha }_{2}\right) \Delta T \implies \left({\alpha }_{1} + {\alpha }_{2}\right) \Delta T = 2{\alpha }_{eq} \Delta T \implies {\alpha }_{eq} = \frac{{\alpha }_{1} + {\alpha }_{2}}{2}$

`

questions.question: If ${K}_{1}$ and ${K}_{2}$ are the thermal conductivities ${L}_{1}$ and ${L}_{2}$ are the lengths and ${A}_{1}$ and ${A}_{2}$ are the cross sectional areas of steel and copper rods respectively such that $\frac{{K}_{2}}{{K}_{1}} = 9,\frac{{A}_{1}}{{A}_{2}} = 2,\frac{{L}_{1}}{{L}_{2}} = 2$. Then, for the arrangement as shown in the figure. The value of temperature $T$ of the steel - copper junction in the steady state will be
questions.explanation: At steady state, the heat conducted by both the rods will be the same. The rate of heat conduction is given by, $\frac{dQ}{dt} = \frac{KA}{l} \Delta T$. Therefore, if the temperature of the junction is $T$, $\frac{{K}_{1}{A}_{1}}{{l}_{1}}\left({T}_{1} - T\right) = \frac{{K}_{2}{A}_{2}}{{l}_{2}}\left(T - {T}_{2}\right) \implies \frac{450 - T}{T - 0} = \frac{{K}_{2}{A}_{2}{l}_{1}}{{K}_{1}{A}_{1}{l}_{2}} = 9 \times \frac{1}{2} \times 2 \implies 450 - T = 9T\;$ `

questions.question:
Two cylindrical rods A and B made of different materials, are joined in a straight line. The ratio of lengths, radii and thermal conductivities of these rods are :

$\frac{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}}=\frac{1}{2}, \frac{\mathrm{r}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{r}_{\mathrm{B}}}=2$ and $\frac{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{B}}}=\frac{1}{2}$. The free ends of rods A and B are maintained at $400 \mathrm{~K}, 200 \mathrm{~K}$, respectively. The temperature of rods interface is ________ K, when equilibrium is established.
questions.explanation: $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{R}_1=\frac{\ell_1}{\mathrm{~K}_1 \mathrm{~A}_1}, \mathrm{R}_2=\frac{\ell_2}{\mathrm{~K}_2 \mathrm{~A}_2} \\ & \frac{\mathrm{dQ}}{\mathrm{dt}}=\frac{\Delta \mathrm{T}}{\mathrm{R}} \\ & \left(\frac{\mathrm{dQ}}{\mathrm{dt}}\right)_1=\left(\frac{\mathrm{dQ}}{\mu}\right)_2 \\ & \frac{400-\mathrm{T}}{\mathrm{R}_1}=\frac{\mathrm{T}-200}{\mathrm{R}_2} \\ & \frac{400-\mathrm{T}}{\mathrm{T}-200}=\frac{\mathrm{R}_1}{\mathrm{R}_2}=\left(\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_2}\right)\left(\frac{\mathrm{r}_2}{\mathrm{r}_1}\right)^2 \times \frac{\mathrm{K}_2}{\mathrm{~K}_1} \\ & =\frac{1}{2} \times\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 \times 2 \\ & =\left(\frac{1}{4}\right) \\ & \frac{400-\mathrm{T}}{\mathrm{T}-200}=\frac{1}{4} \\ & 1600-4 \mathrm{~T}=\mathrm{T}-200 \\ & 5 \mathrm{~T}=1800 \\ & \mathrm{~T}=360 \mathrm{~K}\end{aligned}$

questions.question: Resistance of the wire is measured as $2\Omega$ and $3\Omega$ at $10 ^\circ C$ and $30 ^\circ C$ respectively. Temperature coefficient of resistance of the material of the wire is
questions.explanation:
Resistance of a material is related to temperature by expression $R = {R}_{0}\left(1 + \alpha \Delta T\right)$

Here, at $10 ^\circ C$, we have $2 = {R}_{0}\left(1 + 10\alpha \right)...\left(i\right)$

And at $30 ^\circ C$, we have $3 = {R}_{0}\left(1 + 30\alpha \right)...\left(ii\right)$

From equation $\left(i\right)$, ${R}_{0} = \frac{2}{\left(1 + 10\alpha \right)}$

Putting this value in equation $\left(ii\right)$,

$3 = \frac{2}{1 + 10\alpha }\left(1 + 30\alpha \right)\; \implies 1 = 30\alpha$

Hence, temperature coefficient of the material of wire is $\alpha = \frac{1}{30} = 0.033 ^\circ {C}^{ - 1}$

They are joined together at their ends to make a long rod (see figure). One end of the long rod is maintained at $100 ^\circ C$ and the other at $0 ^\circ C$ (see figure). If the joints of the rod are at $70 ^\circ C$ and $20 ^\circ C$ in steady and there is no loss of energy from the surface of the rod, the correct relationship between ${K}_{1},{K}_{2}$ and ${K}_{3}$ is :

A heat source at $T = {10}^{3}K$ is connected to another heat reservoir at $T = {10}^{2}K$ by a copper slab which is $1m$ thick. Given that the thermal conductivity of copper is $0.1W{K}^{ - 1}{m}^{ - 1}$, the energy flux through it in the steady-state is:
questions.explanation:
Given,

Temperature of heat source, ${T}_{H} = {10}^{3}K$,

Temperature of heat reservoir, ${T}_{L} = {10}^{2}K$,

Conductivity of copper $K = 0.1W{K}^{ - 1}{m}^{ - 1}$

From the equation of steady-state heat flow,

$\frac{dQ}{dt} = \frac{KA \Delta T}{L}$

Heat energy flux can be defined as the rate of heat energy transfer through a given surface.

$\frac{1}{A}\left(\frac{dQ}{dt}\right) = K \times \frac{1000 - 100}{1} = 90W{m}^{ - 2}$
